2027-07-05.title: The Seventy-two Heralds · Monday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: The weapons of our warfare have divine power; authority given for building up and not for tearing down
The Lord sends out the seventy-two ahead of him in pairs: the harvest is plentiful, the laborers are few, “Peace to this house!”
2027-07-05.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the commemoration of the Seventy-two Heralds (എഴുപത്തിരണ്ട് അറിയിപ്പുകാർ), the disciples whom the Lord sent ahead of him in Luke 10:1. Yesterday was the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost, and on Saturday the Church kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha.
2027-07-05.verse: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
theo: On the Monday after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost the Panchangam turns to a group whose names we hardly know, the Seventy-two Heralds. St Luke writes: “After this the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go.” The word “others” tells us that these are not the Twelve, whom Luke has just shown being sent out in the previous chapter. As for the number, the manuscripts of the Gospel are divided between seventy and seventy-two, and the Malayalam Bible that we use has seventy-two, as does the Panchangam. Both numbers carry a meaning. The Twelve recall the twelve tribes of Israel; the seventy or seventy-two recall the nations of the earth, which the book of Genesis lists as seventy in its Hebrew text and seventy-two in the old Greek version, and also the seventy elders on whom Moses saw the spirit rest in the wilderness (Numbers 11:24–26). Many Christian writers, ancient and modern, therefore see in this second sending a sign that the Gospel is meant for all peoples. They are called heralds, announcers, because they go ahead: they prepare the towns for the Lord who is coming after them.

Their instructions begin with a surprise. Before saying “Go,” the Lord says “Pray”: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” The mission starts on our knees, and the Lord is the one who sends. Then comes a warning that is plain and without decoration: “See, I am sending you out like lambs into the midst of wolves.” They are to be defenceless and dependent: “Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals; and greet no one on the road.” The last words are not rudeness. On eastern roads a greeting could take hours of ceremony; the heralds have no time to lose. And they go in pairs. St Gregory the Great noticed that the Lord sends his disciples two by two because there are two commandments of love, of God and of neighbour, and love needs at least two (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance). Two people carry the message more truthfully than one, they hold each other up on the road, and their agreement is itself a proof.

Then the Lord describes how the Gospel spreads, and it is through homes. “Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house!’ And if anyone is there who shares in peace, your peace will rest on that person; but if not, it will return to you.” The first word of the herald is a blessing. “Remain in the same house, eating and drinking whatever they provide, for the laborer deserves to be paid. Do not move about from house to house.” They are to stay, to eat what is set before them and to learn the family's life; they are not to go about looking for a more comfortable house. It is a Kerala picture as much as a Galilean one: the family prayer in the evening, the priest's visit to bless the house, the neighbours who take a stranger in. And the message comes with healing: “cure the sick who are there, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’” Care and word go together. Even if a town refuses them, the message stands: “Yet know this: the kingdom of God has come near.” The refusal of some does not cancel the nearness of the kingdom.

The Epistle tells us what kind of weapons such messengers carry. St Paul has been ridiculed in Corinth: they say “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.” He answers: “Indeed, we live as human beings, but we do not wage war according to human standards; for the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power to destroy strongholds.” The heralds' weapons are the word, peace, prayer, patience and the care of the sick, and their aim is “to take every thought captive to obey Christ.” Their authority is “for building you up and not for tearing you down.” Our own Syriac tradition remembers heralds of this kind. Eusebius tells that after the Ascension Thomas sent Thaddaeus, whom he counts “one of the seventy,” to Edessa, where he healed and preached; the Syriac Churches honour him as Mar Addai (Church History 1.13, in substance). And on Saturday we kept the Dukrono of Mar Thoma Shleeha, the Apostle whom tradition says brought the Gospel to India. Every baptized person is also a herald today: Pope Francis wrote that we are no longer to say that we are disciples and missionaries, but always “missionary disciples.” Let us ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers, and let us begin by saying “Peace to this house” at our own door.
outline: Ask: when did I last say a blessing of peace on my own house, and when did I last pray for laborers for the harvest?
The seventy-two go before the Lord to every town; the number points to all the nations; two by two, for love needs two.
The harvest is plentiful and the laborers are few: the mission begins on our knees.
The Gospel spreads through homes, a blessing first, then care of the sick and the word.
Point 4 · Weapons that are not human
Paul's weakness and the divine power of the word; authority to build up, never to tear down.
“The kingdom of God has come near to you.”
live: Pray each day this week, the Our Father and one more prayer, that the Lord of the harvest may send laborers, priests, religious and lay missionaries, into his harvest.
When you come home this week, and when you visit a neighbour, begin by greeting the house with a word of blessing.
Invite a friend to visit with you one sick or lonely person from the parish this week, and bring a word of the Gospel with the visit.
2027-07-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Lord of the harvest, you appointed seventy-two disciples and sent them ahead of you in pairs to every town where you intended to go. Send laborers into your harvest, and make us laborers, lambs among wolves who trust in you alone. Teach us to bless every house we enter with your peace, to eat what is set before us and to care for the sick, and to say to everyone that the kingdom of God has come near. Give us the weapons that have divine power, the word of truth and the gentleness of patience, and let us use any authority only to build up. Through the prayers of the Seventy-two Heralds, of Mar Addai and of Mar Thoma Shleeha, make our Church a herald of your coming. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the end of the Holy Qurbono the people are sent out in peace, like the Seventy-two; what was received at the altar, the Word and the Body of the Lord, is carried into our homes and workplaces, and the peace that rests on us is to rest on every house we enter.
conn: Mark 6:7: the Twelve are sent “two by two”; Acts 13:2–3: Barnabas and Saul are set apart and sent by the Holy Spirit; Luke 10:1: the seventy-two go in pairs to every place the Lord intends to visit.

Numbers 11:24–26: the spirit rests on seventy elders, and also on Eldad and Medad in the camp; Genesis 10: the table of the nations; Luke 10:17: the seventy return with joy, and the Lord tells them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.

Isaiah 52:7: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news”; Matthew 9:37–38: the same saying about the harvest and the laborers; John 4:35–38: the fields are ripe for harvest and the sower and reaper rejoice together.
fathers: The Lord sends the disciples two by two because there are two precepts of charity, to love God and to love our neighbour; and “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” cannot be said without sorrow, for there are many to hear and few to preach (Homilies on the Gospels 17, in substance).
After the Ascension Judas Thomas sent Thaddaeus, one of the seventy disciples of the Lord, to Edessa, where he healed the sick and preached the word of Christ (Church History 1.13, in substance).
magis: The Church is sent by her founder to all nations; the missionary mandate is a command of her own essential universality, and she strives to preach the Gospel to all (in substance).
The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature, since she draws her origin from the mission of the Son and the mission of the Holy Spirit according to the plan of God the Father (in substance).

Every baptized person, whatever his or her role in the Church, is an agent of evangelization; we are no longer to say that we are disciples and missionaries, but rather that we are always missionary disciples (in substance).

quick: The Lord appoints seventy-two others and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town where he intends to go.
He tells them to pray for laborers, to bring peace to every house, to heal the sick and to say that the kingdom of God has come near.
St Paul says that the weapons of the messengers of Christ are not human; they have divine power, and authority is given for building up.
2027-07-05.action: Greet your own house with a blessing of peace when you enter it today, and pray for laborers for the harvest.
2027-07-05.question: Where is the Lord sending me ahead of him, and with whom?
term: From the Syriac word for “one who is sent”. The Panchangam calls the Seventy-two “heralds” (അറിയിപ്പുകാർ), those who announce; in Syriac usage the word shliho is used for the Twelve and for Paul, but the idea is the same for all who are sent by Christ with the message.

family.explain: Jesus once sent seventy-two of his friends to go ahead of him to the towns where he was going to visit. He sent them in pairs, so that no one would walk alone. They carried nothing but the good news. When they came to a house, the first thing they said was: “Peace to this house!” They stayed, ate what was given, and helped the sick. Then they told everyone: the kingdom of God is near. These friends of Jesus are called heralds, because they announced that he was coming. We can be heralds too, whenever we bring peace into a house.
family.intention: We pray for priests, sisters and missionaries, and for ourselves, that we may bring peace wherever we go.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom shall we greet with a word of peace this week?”

illus: In a parish near Pathanamthitta there was a custom, started by an old catechism teacher, that on the Monday after the first heavy rain two parishioners, always a pair, one grown and one young, walked from house to house along the parish road with a single question: has your roof held? They collected nothing and sold nothing. At each door they said a short prayer of peace on the house, and if the roof had leaked, they noted it and sent a word to the parish council. After some years people no longer called these the roof visits; they called them the peace visits. A family that had stopped coming to church because of a quarrel told the visitors that they had been moved by being asked such a small question by two people who had walked in the rain, and they came back the next Sunday.

pm.open: Lord of the harvest, you send us ahead of you to every house and every town. Teach us to pray for laborers, to carry peace, and to say with joy that your kingdom has come near. Amen.
share: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few (Luke 10:2). For which laborers do I pray, and do I ever answer the call myself?
Whatever house you enter, first say, Peace to this house (Luke 10:5). What would it change if I began every visit and every arrival with a blessing?
The weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power (2 Corinthians 10:4). Which weapons do I trust, and which does the Lord ask me to use?
pm.resp: Lord, send laborers into your harvest.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a herald of the kingdom of God in every town and village.
For priests, sisters, catechists and missionaries sent far from home, that the Lord may protect them.
For our parish, that we may carry peace into every house and care for the sick and the lonely.
For all who have been refused a welcome, that they may not lose heart.
For those who have not yet heard the Gospel, that the Lord may send them heralds.
pm.close: Father, you sent your Son and you send us in his name. Give us the peace of your kingdom to carry to every house, and keep us lambs who trust in you in the midst of the wolves. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

kidsaint: An old story told by Eusebius says that King Abgar of Edessa was very ill and had heard about Jesus and his healings. After the Lord had gone up to heaven, one of the seventy disciples, Thaddaeus, was sent to the city. He prayed for the sick, spoke about Jesus and was welcomed. In the Syriac Churches he is remembered as Mar Addai. Lesson: when the Lord sends us, we only need to go with peace and a kind heart, and he will do the rest.

homily: Dear friends, today the Panchangam remembers the Seventy-two Heralds. St Luke tells that the Lord appointed others, seventy or seventy-two in number, and sent them on ahead of him in pairs to every town and place where he himself intended to go (Luke 10:1). They are not the Twelve. They stand for all who are sent to announce that the Lord is coming, and the number reminds us of all the nations of the earth.

The first instruction is to pray: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest (Luke 10:2). Then they are sent as lambs among wolves, with no purse, no bag and no sandals, and in pairs, so that no one goes alone. They are to say first: Peace to this house! (Luke 10:5). They are to eat what is set before them, to cure the sick, and to say: The kingdom of God has come near to you (Luke 10:9).

St Paul tells the Corinthians that the weapons of our warfare are not merely human, but they have divine power (2 Corinthians 10:4). The Lord's heralds do not fight with force but with peace, with the word, with prayer and with the care of the sick. The authority given to them is for building up and not for tearing down (2 Corinthians 10:8).

Every baptized person is a herald. So let us pray for laborers for the harvest, let us greet our homes with a blessing of peace, and let us go, in pairs if we can, to someone who needs to hear that the kingdom of God is near. Amen.
kids: Children, once Jesus sent seventy-two of his friends to go ahead of him to the villages. They went in pairs, so nobody was alone. Do you know the first thing they said when they came to a house? “Peace to this house!” That is a beautiful greeting, isn't it? You can do the same: when you come home, say a happy hello and wish peace to your family. And you can ask a friend to go with you when you visit a grandparent or a neighbour who is sick. Then you will be a herald of Jesus, just like those seventy-two!

intro: Theme: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
On Monday of the seventh week after Pentecost, the commemoration of the Seventy-two Heralds: sent in pairs, sent with peace, and armed with weapons that are not merely human.

sub: Seventy-two others, ahead of the Lord to every town.

Two by two, because love needs two.
q: Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And I said, “Here am I; send me!”
As the Father has sent me, so I send you.
points.apply: Ask the Lord where he is sending you ahead of him this week, and find one companion to go with you.

points.apply: Pray every day this week for laborers for the harvest, and ask whether the Lord is calling you.

Eat what is set before you and care for the sick.

points.h: Weapons that are not merely human
sub: Paul called weak in person and strong in letters.
The word as the sword of the Spirit.
Authority for building up, not tearing down.
q: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, says the Lord of hosts.
Take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
points.apply: Before you answer someone who has hurt you or argued with you this week, say a short prayer for them and speak to build up.

concl: The Lord sends heralds in pairs, with peace and the word, to every town and every house, and the weapons they carry are not merely human.
Every baptized person is a herald: let us pray for laborers and begin by greeting our own house.
2027-07-05.resolve: Pray for laborers, bless every house you enter with peace, and say with joy that the kingdom of God has come near.
